started within a year or two of first periods.

improves with age and after childbirth.

pain with sex (deep), with bowel movements or urination during periods.

von Willebrand disease if heavy since the first period.

Endometriosis: heat, NSAIDs, pelvic-floor physiotherapy, pacing, but these manage, they don’t treat.

Period pain not controlled by NSAIDs and heat, or that interferes with school, work or sleep.

cycles longer than 35 days, fewer than 9 a year, or absent for 3 months (PCOS, thyroid, pregnancy, low body weight).
heavy bleeding by the definitions above or any anaemia.
PMS that disrupts relationships or work.
trying to conceive for a year (6 months over 35).
any bleeding between periods or after sex that recurs.

Sudden severe one-sided pelvic pain, especially with a positive or possible pregnancy test.
faintness, shoulder-tip pain or collapse with pelvic pain or bleeding.
bleeding soaking a pad every 30 minutes with dizziness.
fever with pelvic pain (PID or infected miscarriage).

Endometriosis was being described microscopically (Cullen, 1896 to 1920) but not named until Sampson in 1932.

What it does: Bed rest and avoidance of exertion and ‘brain-work’ during periods.
ergot and hydrastis (goldenseal) for heavy bleeding.
bromides, opium and cannabis tincture for pain; ‘female tonics’ and Lydia Pinkham’s Vegetable Compound (herbs in 20% alcohol).

pregnancy prescribed as a cure for endometriosis-type pain.

hormonal contraception used continuously to stop cycles.

ultrasound and hysteroscopy instead of blind D&C.

How it sees it: Chinese medicine built an entire specialty on the cycle: period pain is blood stasis (sharp, clots) or cold in the uterus (cramping, relieved by heat).

rest and warmth during the bleed.

the long-term stakes, bone and heart, are as important as the hot flushes.

protein at every meal, resistance training, and treating blood pressure and cholesterol early, menopause is the moment heart risk starts to catch up with men’s.

vaginal oestrogen for dryness and recurrent UTIs.
a DEXA scan if risk factors.

a thyroid check at the start.

Anatomy we got wrong — the rete ovarii and other late discoveries.
What you’ll be able to do: Know the rete ovarii, the ‘new organ’ of 2025, what it is and what it might do.
know the other parts of women’s anatomy that were missed, mis-drawn or dismissed until recently.
and understand why: medicine studied the male body as the default.
Women’s bodies have been described by male anatomists on male templates for most of medical history.
The result is a list of structures that were overlooked, drawn wrongly, or declared useless, and then rediscovered.
This section is less about symptoms than about why the first four sections were so late to be taken seriously, and what the newest research says.
When it was properly described: Identified in 1870 (Waldeyer), dismissed as a useless embryonic leftover for 150 years.

whether it works the same in humans and what removing it does are still unknown, this is the beginning of the story, not a treatment.

In ancient Egypt, a scribe called Ahmes copied out a long scroll of maths problems.
To multiply, Egyptians doubled and doubled again, then added up the rows they needed.

In India, the mathematician Brahmagupta wrote rules for using zero as a number.
Indian place value, where a digit’s place says if it means ones, tens or hundreds, travelled with Arab scholars to Europe. We still call our digits Hindu–Arabic numerals.

The Maya wrote numbers with dots and bars. A dot is one, a bar is five, and a shell means zero.

Some people multiplied by halving one number and doubling the other, over and over, writing two columns.

Half as many lots, each twice as big, is the same amount: 4 × 6 is the same as 2 × 12.

In ancient China, people did sums with small rods laid out on a counting board.

Rows of rods are rows of blocks: 3 rows of 4 rods is 3 × 4.

Lattice multiplication was used in the Islamic world, and in Italy it was called gelosia, after the lattice on a window.
You split the numbers into their digits, multiply each pair in a box of the grid, then add along the diagonals.
It’s the same as splitting: 23 × 4 is 20 × 4 and 3 × 4, added up.
In the Yoruba language, many numbers are said by taking away from a twenty.
Fifteen is said as twenty less five, and nineteen as twenty less one.

The Inca kept records on a quipu: many coloured cords, with knots tied along them.
Where a knot sat on the cord showed its place, ones, tens or hundreds, and a gap meant zero.
It’s our place value in knots: 3 knots in the tens and 4 in the ones is 34.
3 knots high on the cord: 3 tens, 30.
4 knots low on the cord: 4 ones.
